sections.h2: What the clerk does when a house sells
sections.html:
In Louisiana's parishes (what other states call counties), the clerk doubles as parish recorder. Deeds, mortgages and other property papers become public record at the recording desk, which is the office buyers, sellers, title companies and heirs all end up dealing with.

A deputy clerk stamps each incoming document with a unique instrument number plus an index book and page number, and the stamp records the date, hour and minute of filing.

Under Civil Code article 3346, an instrument creating or relating to a mortgage or privilege on land goes into the parish mortgage records. Every other instrument, an act of sale included, goes into the conveyance records. One closing in Livingston Parish can therefore put papers into both sets of books.

The main office is at 20300 Government Blvd., Livingston, LA 70754, mailing address P. O. Box 1150. Call 225-686-2216 or fax 225-686-1867. A satellite office in Denham Springs sits at 145 Del Orleans Avenue, Bldg. 2, Suite E, 70726. Phone ahead to confirm it takes recordings.

Hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The office closes on legal holidays, so plan any closing near these remaining 2026 dates around them:

  • Thursday and Friday, November 26 and 27 (Thanksgiving and the day after)
  • Thursday, December 24, Friday, December 25 and Thursday, December 31

A deed or mortgage of one to five pages costs $125 to record. Longer documents cost more, and a few extras apply to indexing and to badly formatted papers.

ServiceFee
Recording, pages 1 to 5$125.00
Recording, pages 6 to 25$225.00
Recording, pages 26 to 50$325.00
Indexing, first ten names per bookIncluded
Each additional name per book$5
Copies, per page$1.00
Certified copy$10.00
Conformed copy$5.00
Cancellation of mortgage, original note$35.00
Cancellation with affidavit$75.00

Schedules can change, so ask the office for the current total before closing. Your title company or closing attorney normally submits the deed, so ask them to confirm the page count, the number of names and whether both mortgage and conveyance books are involved.

The fee schedule covers recording, indexing, copy, map and cancellation charges. It has no per-dollar transfer tax. What the clerk collects pays for handling pages and names, not a percentage of your price. Mortgage payoff and unpaid property tax are settled between the parties and the title company.

Louisiana statutes set the format, and a document that misses it can draw an extra $10 noncompliance fee. Under R.S. 13:844(D)(1), the first page must be captioned by type of act, with a two inch margin at the top, one inch at the bottom and sides, and type no smaller than eight point. Multiple indebtedness mortgages follow the same rule under R.S. 9:5217(B).

  • Caption the first page with the type of act.
  • Leave the margins described above.
  • Use type of eight point or larger.
  • Do not expect the original back. Originals are not returned and become part of the parish archives.

For proof of what you filed, ask at filing for a certified copy with the clerk's endorsement.

The mortgage section issues certificates and cancels mortgage inscriptions, and both begin with a written request. Louisiana law requires certificate requests in writing, and the office takes them by fax too. Name the exact people to check and give a legal property description.

A mortgage certificate, properly called a certificate of non-mortgage, is not a title opinion and says nothing about who owns the property. It lists what is recorded against the names searched.

Since July 1, 2006, a borrower who pays off a mortgage on Livingston Parish real estate is responsible for seeing that the mortgage is cancelled. The office needs the original note marked "paid" on its face and will not take faxes or copies. If the note is lost, go back to the lender. Lost note affidavits have mostly given way, under R.S. 44:109, to an authentic act from a financial institution.

A mortgage paid years ago but never cancelled can surface late in a sale. Check the mortgage records early so there is time to fix it.

The conveyance section lets the public research property transactions, mineral leases, restrictions and subdivision maps through written or computerized indexes dating back to 1875. Large-screen computer stations serve real estate agents, surveyors, appraisers, abstractors and attorneys, and staff help is free.

Surveys cause trouble. Louisiana law does not require a survey of conveyed property to be recorded or separately indexed, so some were never recorded or cannot be found. The mapping section keeps a map index showing for whom a map was prepared, the property size, its location and the surveyor, and a surveyor may hold a copy the clerk lacks.

For ownership lines, use the parish ownership map on livingstonassessor.com.

Livingston Parish lies east of Baton Rouge. Denham Springs, Walker, Livingston, Albany and Springfield are its towns and cities, and the main clerk's office is in the town of Livingston, the parish seat. It is one of the fastest-growing parishes in the state, with Interstate 12 as its east-west route.

The August 2016 flood still comes up in nearly every house conversation. A state economic impact report estimated that 38,300 of the parish's 52,104 housing units flooded. The Amite River gauge at Denham Springs lists August 14, 2016 as the flood of record. Sellers will see it in three ways:

  • Buyers and lenders ask whether the house took water, what was rebuilt and who did the work.
  • Elevation, flood zone and insurance history become part of price talks.
  • Repair records, permits and contractor payments help answer those questions.

A flood-history house that still needs work is a common reason owners consider an as-is sale over repairing and listing.

sections.h2: Heirs and owners with a distressed house
sections.html:
Start with the recorded history. Pull the conveyance records for the last transfer, then the mortgage records for open liens. A clean record of who owns the house and what is owed makes any sale, cash or otherwise, move faster.

If the owner died, the paperwork that moves title to heirs is a court or affidavit process described in our Louisiana estate tax guide, and it ends with a document that goes to the same recording desk. For rentals, see our guides on the eviction process and the eviction notice.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Livingston Parish?
faqs.a: At the Livingston Parish Clerk of Court's recording desk, 20300 Government Blvd., Livingston, LA 70754. A Denham Springs satellite office exists, but phone first to confirm it takes recordings. The main number is 225-686-2216.

faqs.q: How much is the recording fee for a short deed in Livingston Parish?
faqs.a: It is $125 for pages 1 to 5, $225 for pages 6 to 25 and $325 for pages 26 to 50, with the first ten names per book included in indexing. Check with the office for the current total.

faqs.q: Does the Livingston Parish clerk return the original deed?
faqs.a: No. Originals become part of the parish archives. You can request a certified copy with the clerk's endorsement at filing.

faqs.q: Who cancels a paid-off mortgage in Livingston Parish?
faqs.a: The borrower is responsible. Since July 1, 2006, the borrower, not the lender, bears the risk if a paid mortgage is never cancelled, and the office needs the original note marked paid.

faqs.q: Can I sell a flood-damaged Livingston Parish house as-is?
faqs.a: Yes, but expect buyers to ask for repair, permit and insurance history. Get your recorded title and mortgage payoff in order first so the record does not slow the sale.
